answer.exemplar: The rule that assigns clinics knows only the clinic list, so every characteristic of every clinic, measured or not, is spread across the arms by the same process. Anything that would otherwise sit alongside the treatment and drive missed appointments lands about equally in both arms and largely cancels from the contrast, which leaves the scheduling system as the only systematic difference between them. An observational comparison has no version of this guarantee, since a factor that both separates the groups and moves the outcome stays attached to the treatment no matter how carefully the data are later modelled. That guarantee, not the sample size or the p-value, is what the design bought.

questions.explanation: Random assignment acts on every characteristic of the clinics at once, recorded or not, because the rule that sorts them knows none of them. With enough clinics each unmeasured factor lands roughly evenly in both arms, so whatever it does to missed appointments it does about equally, and the leftover gap is the scheduling system's doing. An observational comparison enjoys no such bargain: a factor that both separates the arms and drives appointments stays welded to the contrast, and no model fitted afterwards can tell it apart from the treatment.

answer.exemplar: An effect is always an effect in some population, on some outcome, over some horizon, so a target left unstated can afterwards be read in whichever of those ways flatters the result. Stating the estimand before the analysis turns each of those into a commitment rather than a reading chosen once the numbers are visible. It costs a paragraph and it is the cheapest safeguard available to a study.

questions.explanation: A causal effect is always an effect for a particular group, on a particular outcome, over a particular period, and a result reported without those three is a claim waiting to be completed by the reader. If the four outcomes were independent, the chance that at least one clears 5 percent is about 19 percent, and correlated outcomes change that number without removing the problem. The honest presentation reports all four, names the one designated primary beforehand if there was one, and labels the rest as exploratory rather than choosing between them after the fact.
questions.hint: Ask whether the threshold or the outcome was chosen first.

questions.explanation: The requirement is exclusion: the reform must have no route to reading scores other than class size. The analysis can do a great deal about the other assumption, that the reform moved class size strongly, by reporting the first stage and its standard error. It can do nothing whatever about exclusion, because the same bundle of changes is produced under every rival route the reform opened, and no sample size changes that. The defensible move is to write the exclusion argument out as an assumption about the world, list the alternatives the reform plausibly carried, and let the reader weigh it.
questions.hint: One instrumental assumption can be measured and the other can only be argued.
questions.learningObjective: state the exclusion restriction and what data cannot do about it

The reform must have been allocated at random, which the schools chosen reveal directly

options.misconception: believes pre-period scores test the exclusion restriction

options.text: The reform must have improved every other school input too, so the rise is properly attributed
options.misconception: reverses the requirement into something that confirms the claim

questions.explanation: A randomly assigned unit is one whose treatment was drawn, and here that is the school, so the design holds thirty draws and no more. The 750 pupils inherit their treatment from those thirty and cannot add independent information, which is what the intraclass correlation of 0.10 quantifies: pupils in one school resemble each other far more than pupils in different schools. The design effect of 1 plus 24 times 0.10, which is 3.4, turns 750 nominal observations into about 220 effective ones, and the analysis must use the second figure.
questions.hint: Only the things that were tossed count as independent draws.

options.text: One assignment, and the study has 30, so the analysis can safely pool all pupils across the schools

answer.exemplar: Adherence was decided by the participants after they were randomised, and people who follow a regimen differ beforehand in illness severity, health habits and motivation. Each of those differences moves blood pressure directly as well as through the medicine, so an adherence contrast carries all of them along with the drug. The randomisation licenses the comparison between the assigned groups and nothing else, because adherence was never randomised. The excess of the adherer contrast over the randomised one is therefore a rough gauge of how strong that selection is, and a large excess is a warning rather than a finding.

questions.explanation: The trial randomised the medicine, not the taking of it, and the two differ. People who adhere differ from people who do not in ways that predate the prescription and that affect blood pressure on their own, so the adherer contrast blends the drug's effect with everything that made adherers different in the first place. A clean version of the question would ask what would have happened to the same people had they been told to take a different share of tablets, and nobody has run that trial. The gap between the two contrasts measures the selection, not the adherence.
questions.hint: Assignment was randomised; adherence was chosen afterwards.
questions.learningObjective: explain why an adherence contrast is not a causal effect

answer.exemplar: Each verdict is a statement about an interval, not about the world, and two intervals that overlap are perfectly compatible with one common value. The men's interval may sit entirely above no effect while the women's straddles it, which is what a moderate true effect produces when one subgroup is larger than the other. The only thing that addresses the question directly is a test of the difference between the two estimates against its own standard error, and that test is usually much weaker than the pair of verdicts suggests. Since the subgroup was not pre-specified, whatever it finds is exploratory and should be labelled so.

questions.explanation: A significant result and a non-significant result are not opposites, and the distance between them is not a measured difference. Both verdicts come with intervals, and a single moderate effect will clear the threshold in the larger subgroup and not in the smaller without any real heterogeneity existing. What settles the question is testing the difference between the two estimates directly, which needs its own standard error and is a much less impressive calculation than the two verdicts suggest. A subgroup chosen after the data were seen makes the whole exercise exploratory besides.
questions.hint: Two verdicts are not one comparison, and only the comparison tests the difference.
questions.learningObjective: explain why two subgroup verdicts do not establish an interaction

answer.exemplar: Mentoring is taken up after the randomisation by people who were already more engaged, and that engagement is exactly what makes them improve more. Regressing the outcome on the indicator therefore compares trainees who differ on the indicator and on the motivation behind it, holding fixed part of what the training was supposed to produce. Whenever the covariate carries part of the treatment's effect, this shrinks the treatment coefficient towards zero by an amount that is not a correction but a removal. The assigned-group contrast is the number the design licenses, and the mentoring pattern belongs in the paper as a hypothesis about mechanism rather than as a control.

questions.explanation: The covariate was chosen by the trainees after allocation, so it is a consequence of how the training landed rather than a background characteristic. Adjusting for it compares engaged trainees with disengaged ones and strips away part of the very effect being estimated, which is why the coefficient falls. Nothing is being corrected for here; a piece of the treatment's effect is simply being held at a constant value. The randomised comparison of assigned groups remains the estimate that means what the design says it means.
questions.hint: Ask whether the covariate was assigned, or was taken up afterwards.
questions.learningObjective: explain why a post-treatment covariate distorts an estimate

questions.explanation: The outcome and the analysis are committed to before recruitment, because that is the whole mechanism by which later choices cannot chase the data. Randomisation comes next, and it is what makes the later comparison mean something, so everything downstream of it is interpretation rather than a further choice. Delivering the treatment and keeping assessors unaware comes after allocation, since a participant cannot be treated before being assigned. Follow-up as assigned closes the design, because dropping people after allocation is the step that most often undoes a randomisation. The final comparison on the pre-specified analysis is a report of what the design produced, not a fresh analysis.
questions.hint: The commitment that cannot be taken back has to come before the data exist.
questions.learningObjective: sequence the conduct and reporting of a randomised trial

options.text: Fix the outcome, the exclusion rules and the analysis before anybody is allocated
Recruit and consent participants, then randomise them to the study arms
Deliver the assigned treatment and keep participants and assessors unaware where feasible
Follow every participant as allocated and record outcomes, including for those who stop
Compare the arms on the pre-specified analysis, reporting the interval and the attrition

questions.explanation: The diagram comes first because every later step is a reading of it, and a reader who skips it is adjusting on grounds that were never argued. Only once the structure is written down can the adjustment sets be identified, since the same covariate blocks a back-door in one structure and opens a collider in another. Overlap comes after the sets are chosen, because it is a property of the data that a set may simply fail. Estimation follows balance, and a large standardised difference on an adjusted variable is a warning that the earlier steps were not right. The sensitivity analysis is last, and it is the only step that says what the estimate cannot rule out.
questions.hint: Nothing is adjusted for until the structure that justifies the adjustment is written down.

questions.explanation: The units, the outcome and the policy date are fixed before the plot is read, because a window that starts where the trends happen to diverge is a window chosen to help. The pre-policy comparison comes next and is the only direct evidence available for parallel trends, which is why it is examined before the estimate rather than after. The counterfactual is then projected forward from each unit's own untreated path, and the difference of the two changes follows from that. The placebo comparison on untreated units is last, and it can reveal a design problem that no amount of care with the main specification would have shown.

Take the difference between the two changes to get the estimate and an interval for it
Rerun the same comparison on units the policy never touched as a check on the design

questions.explanation: The first-stage diagnostic is arithmetic and belongs at the front, because a weak instrument makes everything after it uninterpretable however carefully the rest is done. The exclusion argument comes next, and unlike the diagnostic it is not a calculation but a case about the world, which is why it belongs in the text rather than in a table. The second-stage estimate is then read with an interval that reflects the first stage, since the usual standard error is wrong when the instrument is weak. The range of the instrument's own values defines which comparisons the estimate actually speaks for. Sensitivity to other candidate instruments is last, and it is what converts a single fragile number into an assessment.
questions.hint: One assumption can be checked arithmetically and the other only argued.
questions.learningObjective: sequence the steps of an instrumental variable analysis

options.text: Check that the instrument moves the treatment strongly, using the first stage and its F statistic
Set out the argument that the instrument shifts the outcome only through the treatment
Estimate the second stage and read the effect with an interval that carries the first stage
Report the range of the instrument's own values, since that bounds the identified variation
Show how the estimate moves under weak instruments and under other candidate instruments
